title: Olbers' Paradox: Why Is the Night Sky Dark?
question: If the universe is infinite, eternal, and full of stars, why isn't every point in the night sky blazing with light?
summary: A childishly simple observation — the sky is dark at night — turns out to encode deep facts about the age, size, and expansion of the universe, and stumped astronomers for two centuries before cosmology could explain it.
content:
Go outside on a clear, moonless night and look up. Between the stars, the sky is dark. This seems too obvious to be interesting — of course it's dark, space is mostly empty. But run the numbers on an infinite, eternal, uniformly star-filled universe, and something strange happens: the night sky should be blindingly bright, not dark. This is Olbers' Paradox, named for the German astronomer Heinrich Olbers who popularized it in 1823, though the puzzle traces back further, including a striking early treatment by Edgar Allan Poe in his 1848 prose poem "Eureka."

The Naive Argument for a Bright Sky

Imagine the universe is infinite in extent, eternal in time, and stars are scattered through it at roughly uniform density. Divide space into thin concentric shells centered on Earth. A shell twice as far away contains four times as much surface area, so it contains roughly four times as many stars — but each of those stars appears one-quarter as bright due to the inverse-square law of light. The two effects cancel exactly: every shell, no matter how distant, contributes the same total brightness to the sky. Add up infinitely many shells, each contributing equally, and you get infinite brightness. Every line of sight, in every direction, should eventually terminate on the surface of some star, meaning the entire sky should look as bright as the surface of the Sun. Yet clearly it doesn't.

Resolution 1: The Universe Has a Finite Age

The dominant resolution is almost embarrassingly simple once you have modern cosmology: the universe is not eternal. It's about 13.8 billion years old, and light travels at a finite speed. That means we can only ever see light that has had time to reach us — a finite observable universe, not an infinite one. Beyond a certain distance (the cosmic horizon), there hasn't been enough time since the Big Bang for any light to arrive yet, no matter how many stars might exist out there. The infinite sum in the naive argument gets cut off before it can diverge.

Resolution 2: Expansion, Redshift, and a Finite Stellar Lifetime

Even within the observable universe, several other effects reduce the sky's brightness. The universe is expanding, so light from very distant sources gets redshifted — stretched to longer, less energetic wavelengths — which dims its effective contribution to visible light. Stars also don't live forever; they form, burn, and die, so at any given moment only a finite number are shining rather than an eternal, unbroken field of light. And on the largest scales, matter isn't uniformly distributed — it's clumped into galaxies separated by enormous voids, so many lines of sight simply miss stars altogether rather than terminating on one, contrary to the paradox's key assumption.

A Simple Observation as Cosmological Evidence

What makes Olbers' Paradox remarkable isn't the resolution itself but what the puzzle demonstrates: an observation anyone can make with the naked eye — "it's dark at night" — turns out to be genuine empirical evidence against an infinite, static, eternal universe, decades before Hubble discovered cosmic expansion or anyone had measured the age of the cosmos. Kelvin explored versions of this reasoning in the 19th century, and it stands as one of the earliest examples of cosmology being constrained by pure logic applied to an everyday observation, without a telescope doing anything more sophisticated than passively receiving photons.

What the Dark Sky Still Tells Us

Today, Olbers' Paradox is less a live mystery than a teaching tool — a clean entry point into why the universe must have a beginning in time, a finite age, and an expansion history, all packed into the simple fact of darkness between the stars. It's a reminder that some of the deepest constraints on the structure of reality hide in observations so mundane that for centuries almost no one thought to ask why they were true.

perspectives.title: Astrophysics Perspective
perspectives.description: The finite speed of light combined with the universe's finite age of 13.8 billion years caps how much starlight can have reached us, resolving the paradox's core assumption of infinite accumulated light.

perspectives.title: Cosmology Perspective
perspectives.description: Cosmic expansion redshifts distant light to lower energies, and large-scale voids between galaxy clusters mean not every line of sight terminates on a star, further reducing the sky's total brightness.

perspectives.title: History of Science Perspective
perspectives.description: The paradox was explored well before modern cosmology existed, including by Edgar Allan Poe in 1848, showing how a purely logical puzzle can anticipate empirical discoveries made decades later.

perspectives.title: Philosophy of Science Perspective
perspectives.description: Olbers' Paradox exemplifies how a single, everyday observation can falsify an entire class of cosmological models, illustrating how minimal empirical data can powerfully constrain theory.

openQuestions: If the universe turns out to be truly infinite in spatial extent beyond our observable horizon, does that revive any version of the paradox, or does expansion alone fully resolve it?
How much of the night sky's darkness is due to finite age versus expansion versus large-scale structure, and can these contributions be cleanly separated observationally?
Could an alien civilization with a vastly different vantage point in the universe observe a measurably different sky brightness, and what would that tell us about our position?
What other everyday, naked-eye observations might still be hiding deep cosmological constraints we haven't recognized yet?
